$comment: WORLD DOCUMENT — the retrieval corpus for the Luma competitor round. GENERATED from the capture files; never hand-written. Each entry is a self-contained chunk carrying its own claim, confidence, scope limit and source file. If a chunk and its source disagree, THE SOURCE WINS.
purpose: Retrieval. Each chunk is written to be answerable on its own, so a retrieved fragment never arrives without its confidence or its limits attached. This is deliberate: the failure mode of a RAG corpus is a true sentence retrieved without the caveat that made it true.

authority.this_document: an INDEX of evidence. Not synthesis. No claim here has passed Gate A.
authority.source_of_truth: the capture files under captures/. This document is regenerable from them.

coverage_warning.headline: NO COMPETITOR IS COMPLETE. All 17 touched; none exhausted.
coverage_warning.states: 8 of 119 (6%) — one empty state in the whole round; zero error, no-results or offline
coverage_warning.consequence: Findings on discovery, comparison, ranking, loyalty and pricing rest on broad coverage. Findings on post-purchase, disruption and failure states rest on very little — which is where Luma proposes to differentiate. Weight accordingly.

chunks.claim: Priority support — the benefit a low-confidence traveller needs most — is gated behind 15 completed bookings in 2 years, so it is structurally unreachable by a first-time traveller.
chunks.evidence: Level 3 benefit list includes 'Priority support for stays'; Level 3 qualifying rule is 15 bookings in 2 years, captured verbatim above.

chunks.claim: The Genius programme never addresses a first-time traveller anywhere on its own explainer page.
chunks.scope_limit: Absence on THIS page only. Not evidence of absence across the product.
chunks.evidence: Full page text (5,250 chars) contains no match for 'first-time', 'new to Booking', or 'beginner'.

chunks.claim: The market leader contractually disclaims liability for the exact failure experience a reassurance-led product would want to own — at least for flights.
chunks.scope_limit: Quoted clauses concern FLIGHTS. Accommodation sits under section B with a different contractual relationship, not yet captured.
evidence: We act solely as the Platform and are not involved in the Third-Party Terms. We are not responsible for your ticket or any extras you may buy and (to the fullest extent permitted by law) have no liability to you in relation to your Booking.
Most Flights on our Platform are provided via a Third-Party Aggregator, which acts as an intermediary to the airline(s).

chunks.claim: Booking.com does operate a disruption mechanism, but only where it holds the supplier relationship.
evidence: For any airport pick-up, you must give us your flight details at least 24 hours before your pick-up Time so your Service Provider can adjust the pick-up Time if your flight is delayed.
If your flight is delayed or canceled or you're denied boarding, you may be entitled to compensation/assistance under EU Regulation 261/2004

chunks.claim: Accessibility is a contractual term, not only a design commitment — section A11 'Accessibility requests' sits in the Terms of Service.
The statement names no accessibility standard and makes no conformance claim.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma's own constraint is explicit: WCAG 2.2 AA. The market leader publishes a statement of intent without a testable claim.
chunks.scope_limit: This concerns the WORDING of the published statement. It is not a finding about Booking.com's actual accessibility, which this capture does not test.
chunks.evidence: Searched the full 8,125-character document for WCAG, 'Web Content Accessibility', 'Level A/AA/AAA', 'EN 301 549', 'Section 508' and 'European Accessibility Act'. The only match is the phrase 'aligning with the currently applicable EU standards' — no standard named, no conformance level stated, no 'fully' or 'partially conformant' claim.

chunks.claim: Accessibility of the actual travel experience is routed away from Booking.com to the supplier.
chunks.evidence: If you have any questions about your Travel Experience (wheelchair access, walk-in baths, etc.), contact the service provider of the Travel Experience (including but not limited to the owner of a hotel or other property, a museum or park...)

chunks.claim: Across three first-party documents Booking.com consistently occupies an intermediary position and pushes responsibility outward at every layer.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma's stated goal is owning the traveller's confidence across the whole journey. The incumbent with the widest capability has contractually declined to own the failure moments. That is either the gap Luma fills or the reason nobody has.
evidence: Terms A19 / flights: 'We act solely as the Platform... have no liability to you in relation to your Booking.'
Terms / disruption: statutory EU 261/2004 rights are signposted rather than acted on.
Accessibility Statement: experience-level accessibility questions go to the service provider.
Genius: the one benefit that implies Booking.com acting FOR the traveller — priority support — requires 15 bookings in 2 years.

chunks.claim: Booking.com offers no ranking axis based on effort, ease, stress or traveller confidence. Every axis is price, a quality proxy, distance, property type, or an opaque default.
chunks.scope_limit: Accommodation search only, one market, one query. Flights, cars and attractions have their own sorters — not yet captured.

chunks.claim: Booking.com DOES disclose that commercial terms affect ranking — so a blanket claim that competitors never explain their recommendations does not hold here.
chunks.evidence: Commission paid on bookings, and other factors can affect property rankings. Learn about these ranking parameters and how to select and modify them. Learn more

chunks.claim: Loyalty membership changes the ranking surface by exactly one axis, and that axis is another PRICE axis.
chunks.why_it_matters: Reinforces F-09 from the other direction. Booking.com's loyalty programme does not unlock an ease, effort or confidence axis — it unlocks a further discount axis. Across both states, zero of 11 axes concern how easy a trip will be.
chunks.evidence: Signed out: 10 sort options, no Genius entry. Signed in at Genius Level 2: the same 10 plus 'Genius discounts first'. Result count and ranking disclosure identical.

chunks.claim: Booking.com fires a Google One Tap sign-in prompt at a signed-out user during search.
chunks.evidence: Navigating the signed-out instance to the search results URL opened a Google accounts sign-in page as a second tab.

chunks.claim: The primary Reserve control is inert until a room quantity is selected, and nothing states this.
chunks.why_it_matters: An enabled control that silently does nothing is worse than a disabled one for a low-confidence user, who reads no response as their own error. Luma's stated primary user is exactly this person.
chunks.evidence: On the property page, clicking 'I'll reserve' produced no navigation. After setting a room-quantity <select> to 1 and dispatching change, the identical click advanced to /book.html. The button was never disabled — it was enabled and did nothing.

chunks.claim: No account is required to reach the booking form. There is no sign-in wall and no guest-checkout prompt either — the question is simply never asked.
chunks.why_it_matters: Friction is deferred rather than imposed. Contrast with the Genius finding: the account matters for price, not for permission.
chunks.evidence: At /book.html signed out: no 'sign in', 'create an account' or 'continue as guest' text present. The form is served directly.

chunks.claim: Booking.com's answer to multi-type trip attachment is three opt-in checkboxes inside the booking form.
chunks.decision_for_luma: Decision required: is Luma's multi-type attachment a checkbox at checkout, or a consequence of the trip being modelled as one object? These produce very different products.
chunks.evidence: Form carries checkboxes named interested_flight, interested_car_rentals, interested_taxi.

chunks.claim: Expedia carries six verticals to Booking.com's four booking types, adding Packages and Cruises — but presents a far smaller link surface on the homepage.
chunks.scope_limit: Link count is a proxy for surface breadth, not for capability. Recorded as a measured difference, not a quality judgement.
chunks.evidence: Expedia homepage: 39 links, 1,529 DOM nodes. Booking.com homepage: 300 links, 5,393 DOM nodes. Same capture method, same day, both signed out.

chunks.claim: Romie — named in prior desk research as the most serious competitive threat and the top open question — does not appear anywhere on the Expedia homepage.
chunks.scope_limit: HOMEPAGE ONLY. This is not evidence that Romie does not exist or has not shipped. It establishes that it is not surfaced on the primary entry point. The open question stands until the product surfaces are searched directly.
chunks.evidence: Full homepage text searched for 'romie', case-insensitive, after full render and scroll-to-bottom. No match.

chunks.claim: Both loyalty programmes examined so far gate their better rates behind accumulated bookings, and neither addresses a first-time traveller anywhere on its own explainer page.
evidence: Booking.com Genius: Level 2 = 5 bookings in 2 years; Level 3 = 15 bookings in 2 years. Full page text contains no match for first-time / new to Booking / beginner.
Expedia One Key: Blue 0-4 -> Silver 5-14 -> Gold 15-29 -> Platinum 30+ trip elements. Full page text contains no match for first-time / new member / beginner.

chunks.claim: For an identical city and date range, Expedia returns 499 properties where Booking.com returns 4,194 — roughly an eightfold difference.
chunks.scope_limit: Result counts are not directly comparable without knowing each platform's definition of a listing and its default geographic radius. Expedia's count is scoped to 'Lisbon District'. Recorded as a measured difference requiring interpretation, NOT as a claim that Expedia has 8x less inventory.
chunks.evidence: Both captured 2026-09-04, Lisbon, 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-13, 2 adults, 1 room.

chunks.claim: Expedia offers no ranking axis based on effort, ease, stress or confidence. Enumerated positively from the opened control.
Expedia collapses guest details and payment onto ONE page; Booking.com splits them across two, with no payment field present on its details step.
Expedia's insurance decline option is written as a confession of recklessness rather than a neutral choice.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma's stated business objective is 'reducing travel stress'. The incumbent MANUFACTURES stress at the point of payment and monetises the relief. This is the sharpest available example of the market solving for conversion where Luma proposes to solve for confidence — and it is a direct decision, not an observation.

chunks.claim: Google Travel exposes four decision-support surfaces that neither Booking.com nor Expedia offers anywhere in their accommodation journey.
chunks.why_it_matters: These answer 'should I go, when, and roughly what will it cost' — the scenario's stage 1 'Dream & discover' and the front half of stage 2 'Plan & compare'. The two transactional incumbents begin at a search box and assume the decision is already made. Luma's stated primary user, a first-time traveller with low confidence, has NOT already made it.
chunks.scope_limit: Presence of these surfaces is verified. Their QUALITY and whether they materially help is not tested by this capture.
chunks.evidence: Present as primary navigation on the accommodation search result. Booking.com and Expedia captures of the equivalent surface contain no analogue.

chunks.claim: Google Travel hands off rather than sells. No 'Book on Google' surface was present on the accommodation result.
chunks.evidence: Full page text searched for 'book on google' — no match. The forward control is 'View prices'.

chunks.claim: Google Travel offers three ranking axes: an opaque default, price, and a quality proxy. None concerns effort, ease, stress or confidence.
The product with the richest decision-support layer has the poorest ranking layer.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma proposes to serve a first-time traveller across the WHOLE journey — which means it needs Google's front half and the incumbents' back half, and the axis neither has. That is the shape of the opportunity and also the shape of the difficulty.
chunks.evidence: Google Travel: 4 decision surfaces (Track prices, Where to stay, When to visit, What you'll pay), 3 sort axes. Booking.com: 0 decision surfaces, 11 sort axes. Expedia: 0 decision surfaces, 6 sort axes.

chunks.claim: Google Travel is the only product observed that tells a traveller what a normal price looks like before they search.
chunks.scope_limit: Three competitors. Whether any of the remaining fourteen offers an equivalent is untested.
chunks.evidence: 'What you'll pay' gives typical nightly price by star class with an explicit range, month, and inventory count. Booking.com and Expedia captures contain no equivalent — both present prices only in the context of a specific property, anchored against a struck-through 'previous price'.

chunks.claim: Authentication unlocks exactly one capability on Google Travel, and it is a functional one — persistent price monitoring — not a discount.
Two products, two matched-pair diffs, one extra capability each — but of opposite kinds.
chunks.why_it_matters: Both products ask a traveller to create an account. Booking.com's answer to 'why should I?' is a better price; Google's is a capability that persists between sessions. For a first-time traveller — who has no booking history to convert into a discount — only the second kind of reason is available on day one. This is a directly usable answer to the retention problem F-18 left open.
chunks.scope_limit: Two products. Expedia's logged-out state was not captured, so its diff is OWED and its absence is a real gap in this comparison.

chunks.claim: Google Flights publishes an explicit all-in pricing commitment — the stated opposite of drip pricing.
chunks.why_it_matters: For a first-time traveller the fear is not the headline price, it is what appears at the end. A stated all-in commitment answers that fear before it forms.
chunks.evidence: Prices are final prices and include all taxes and fees, including payment fees for the cheapest common payment method (which may d[iffer]...)

chunks.claim: Google Flights explicitly addresses a traveller who has not decided, in its own copy.
chunks.why_it_matters: Booking.com and Expedia both REQUIRE destination and dates as search inputs — an undecided traveller cannot start. Google treats indecision as the normal starting state and builds tools for it: date grid, price graph, price history, tracking. This is the scenario's stage 1 'Dream & discover', which the transactional incumbents skip entirely.
evidence: Not ready to book yet? Observe price changes for a route or flight and get notified when prices drop.
If your travel plans are flexible, use the form above... then play around with the Date grid

chunks.claim: Google Flights states its ranking criteria in plain language on the result set itself.
chunks.why_it_matters: This materially weakens the prior-round hypothesis that 'no competitor consistently explains its recommendations'. One competitor discloses commercial influence; another names its actual criteria. The claim needs restating before it is reused.
chunks.evidence: Ranked based on price and convenience. Prices include required taxes + fees for 1 adult. Optional charges and bag fees may apply.

chunks.claim: On a live route, Google states whether the current price is normal and when to buy — without requiring a booking, an account, or a commitment.
chunks.why_it_matters: 'Prices are currently typical' is the direct answer to a first-time traveller's central fear — am I being taken advantage of. 'Cheapest time to book is usually now, until Oct 17' converts that into a decision with a deadline. Neither transactional competitor said anything equivalent at any point in either journey captured.
evidence: Prices are currently typical
The cheapest time to book is usually now, until Oct 17
View price history

chunks.claim: Google Flights surfaces a comparison dimension that is neither price, quality proxy, nor distance: carbon emissions, expressed relative to the route average.
chunks.scope_limit: This was observed as a DISPLAYED attribute per result. Whether emissions is a selectable SORT axis was not tested this pass. It is therefore NOT added to the 20-axis running total, which counts enumerated sort options only. OWED.
evidence: Avg emissions
-17% emissions
+30% emissions

chunks.claim: Across 20 enumerated ranking axes on three products, ZERO concern effort, ease, stress or confidence. This was described as the load-bearing finding of the round and the basis of Luma's differentiation.
Emissions is a selectable sort axis, not merely a displayed attribute. F-34's OWED test is settled.
chunks.why_it_matters: A non-price, non-quality, computed, relative axis that is sortable AND explained. This is the closest existing template for how an 'ease' axis would have to work: computed per option, expressed relative to a baseline, and accompanied by an explanation of the estimate.
chunks.evidence: menuitemradio 'Emissions' in the sort menu; per-result values 'Carbon emissions estimate: 115 kilograms. -17% emissions' with a 'Learn more about this emissions estimate' affordance.

chunks.claim: Kayak ships a standalone Flight Tracker at /tracker — a direct analogue of a named Luma core feature.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma's Core Features list includes 'Live flight tracking'. Kayak gives it away free, unbundled from any booking, as a top-level product. Combined with Google's price tracking and price history, two of Luma's named features already exist as free-standing free tools from products that never sell the flight.

chunks.claim: The ad-landing variant renders the same product surface as the clean URL. The tracking parameters produced no observable difference.
chunks.scope_limit: One page, one moment. Not a general claim about Kayak's ad landing pages.
chunks.evidence: Clean URL (inspector, signed out): 3,657 DOM nodes, 487 links. Ad-landing URL (authenticated Chrome): 3,668 DOM nodes, 495 links. Identical decision-aid set, identical title, identical locale.

chunks.claim: Kayak places an 'IA' (AI) entry point directly beside its wordmark in the primary header.
chunks.why_it_matters: Prior desk research recorded 'assistant commoditisation' as a standing risk — that conversational planning is already shipped by competitors. This is first-hand confirmation on a third product, in its most prominent header position. Luma positioning on 'having an AI assistant' is positioning on something the market already treats as table stakes.

chunks.claim: Kayak's AI planner ships a designed empty state. This is the first empty state observed anywhere in the round across four competitors.
chunks.why_it_matters: Every capture so far has recorded empty/error/no-results states as NOT OBSERVED, because transactional flows rarely surface them to a browsing user. The AI surface is where a competitor must design for a user who has nothing yet — which is precisely the state Luma's first-time traveller is permanently in. The empty state is not an edge case for that user; it is their opening screen.
chunks.scope_limit: One empty state, one product, one surface. Error, no-results and offline states remain uncaptured everywhere.
chunks.evidence: Aún no tienes planes de viaje

chunks.claim: Kayak's travel AI accepts photo and file upload as planning input, not just text.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma's Core Features list includes 'Travel documents', 'Boarding passes' and 'Offline itinerary' — all of which are FILES a traveller already holds. A competitor has already built the ingestion path for exactly that content, framed as planning input rather than storage. TripIt's whole product is confirmation ingestion. The pattern of 'give us the document you already have' is occupied from two directions before Luma has built anything.
evidence: Entrada de mensaje de chat
Cargar fotos
Elige otro archivo

chunks.claim: The planner asserts the traveller's location unprompted, and asserted it incorrectly.
chunks.why_it_matters: For a confident traveller a wrong default is a minor annoyance. For Luma's stated user — low confidence, needing reassurance at every step — a product that states something false about them in its opening line spends trust it has not yet earned. And it is presented as a statement ('You are in'), not a question.
chunks.scope_limit: Cause not established. Could be IP geolocation, VPN, account setting or a stale default. Recorded as observed behaviour, NOT as a geolocation defect.
chunks.evidence: Estás en Toronto Todos los aeropuertos

chunks.claim: Kayak's sort control displays the consequence of each choice on the control itself — price AND duration on every tab — so the trade-off is legible before the user commits to a sort.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the single most transferable interaction observed in the round. It is not a new axis — it is making an existing trade-off VISIBLE AT THE POINT OF CHOICE. For a traveller who does not know what a reasonable trade looks like, that is the whole problem, and it costs no new data to build.
chunks.decision_for_luma: Decision required: does Luma's ranking control show what each choice costs? Kayak proves it is possible with two variables. Luma proposes to rank on ease, which is harder to display but the same pattern.

chunks.claim: Two of Kayak's three flight sort axes concern duration, confirming that effort IS ranked in flights on a second product.
Kayak labels paid placements explicitly and in the first person of the advertiser.
chunks.why_it_matters: Three competitors now sit on a visible spectrum of ranking honesty: name the criteria (Google), disclose commercial influence at page level (Booking.com), mark each paid placement (Kayak). Luma has a choice on that spectrum and it is a trust decision, not a compliance one.
evidence: Este es un espacio publicitario de Air Europa. Lo estás viendo...
Este es un espacio publicitario de eDreams. Lo estás viendo...

chunks.claim: From a flight result set, Kayak asks whether the traveller wants bus prices.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario's capability list requires on-site transport at stages 2, 3 and 6, and tier 3 of the roster exists because no tier-1 product was assumed to cover it. Here a tier-1 meta-search prompts cross-modally from air to coach. That partially undercuts the tier-3 argument and must be carried into the roster reasoning rather than ignored — it is evidence AGAINST a position this plan already took.
chunks.evidence: ¿Te interesan los precios de los autobuses?

chunks.claim: Two meta-search products state opposite pricing commitments for the same product category.
chunks.why_it_matters: Baggage is the canonical hidden cost in air travel and the one a first-time traveller is least likely to anticipate. Google commits to an all-in price and names the edge case; Kayak explicitly excludes baggage and warns that some rail and coach prices are incomplete too. Same category, same week, opposite promises.
chunks.scope_limit: Captured on different locales (en vs es-es) — a locale confound is live per D-004. Baggage inclusion policy could in principle vary by market. Flagged; not resolved.

chunks.claim: Kayak sells combined itineraries assembled from separate airlines, each governed by its own conditions, with no single carrier owning the journey.
chunks.decision_for_luma: Decision required: can Luma rank or flag by RECOURSE — is this itinerary protected, and by whom? It is computable from data already visible (single ticket vs self-connect, carrier vs aggregator, cancellation terms). No competitor observed does it. This is a stronger differentiation candidate than 'easiest first'.
chunks.evidence: KAYAK Mix ofrece vuelos desde o hacia un destino con varias aerolíneas, los cuales están sujetos a los requisitos y condiciones de reserva de cada una de ellas

chunks.claim: Kayak's handoff on this result went directly to the airline that operates the flight, not to a reseller.
chunks.why_it_matters: It means the traveller ends up holding a DIRECT carrier booking — with the carrier's own obligations, including EU 261/2004 rebooking duties. The meta-search that never sells has, on this path, delivered the traveller into the MOST protected version of the purchase available.
chunks.scope_limit: One result, one route, one fare. Other Kayak results hand off to OTAs (eDreams and others were present as advertisers on the same page). This is not a claim that Kayak always routes to the operator.

chunks.claim: Within a single Kayak result set, the protection a traveller ends up with varies enormously — and nothing in the ranking, sorting or price display reflects that.
chunks.decision_for_luma: Decision required: this is the clearest evidence yet for a 'protected first' axis. It is computable from data Kayak already holds — it knows whether a result is a Mix, an OTA handoff or a carrier handoff, because it constructs the handoff URL. The information exists and is simply not surfaced. Luma would not need new data to rank on it.

chunks.claim: Crossing the handoff, the traveller loses all trace of the product that sent them and immediately faces a fresh consent gate.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario's problem list opens with 'Comparing flights, transport, accommodation and activities happens in different places and never lines up' and 'Information is spread across multiple apps'. This capture is that problem happening in two clicks: a traveller who compared on Kayak is now on an unfamiliar site, re-consenting to cookies, with no thread back. For a first-time traveller this is the moment confidence is most likely to break.
evidence: Destination page contains no Kayak branding or context (checked: no 'kayak' string in visible text)
OneTrust consent checkboxes (ot-group-id-C0002 through C0005) present on arrival — a second cookie decision within one journey

chunks.claim: Booking.com, Kayak and Rentalcars.com — competitors 1, 4 and 9 on the roster — are all Booking Holdings companies. Verified from first-party statements on two of the three.
chunks.evidence: Independientemente de estos acuerdos, nuestra empresa forma parte de Booking Holdings Inc, que cuenta con otras webs de viaje y ocio como Booking.com, Priceline.com, Agoda.com, Rentalcars.com y Opentable.com.

chunks.claim: Kayak publishes an 18,759-character document explaining how it recommends content and orders results, broken down per vertical.
Three competitors, one browser session, one afternoon — and each asserts a different location for the same traveller.
chunks.why_it_matters: Each product states its guess as fact and none asks. For a confident traveller this is noise. For Luma's stated primary user — low confidence, needing reassurance at every step — three products asserting three different countries is a demonstration that these systems do not actually know them. A product whose entire proposition is trustworthiness cannot afford a confident wrong opening line.
chunks.scope_limit: Cause not established for any of the three. Could be IP, CDN edge, account default, or prior session. Recorded as observed divergence, NOT as a geolocation defect in any product.
evidence: Google Travel AI planner: 'Estás en Toronto Todos los aeropuertos' (F-41)
Kayak: origin pre-filled 'Madrid (MAD)' (F-38 capture)
Skyscanner: 'Salida desde: Marsella (MRS)'

chunks.claim: Skyscanner offers search with no destination at all — 'Explora cualquier lugar'.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the most radical form of the undecided-traveller affordance observed. Google Travel builds 'When to visit' and 'What you'll pay' for a traveller who has picked a place but not a date. Skyscanner removes the destination requirement entirely. Booking.com and Expedia both REQUIRE destination and dates before anything happens.

chunks.claim: Skyscanner's own FAQ headings directly address the confusion the handoff creates.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-50 recorded that crossing the Kayak handoff drops all context — new brand, fresh consent gate, no thread back. Skyscanner evidently knows this is confusing enough to answer as a top-level FAQ. A competitor documenting its own seam is the strongest available evidence that the seam is a real user problem, not an analyst's inference.
evidence: ¿El vuelo se reserva con Skyscanner?
¿Qué ocurre después de reservar un vuelo?
¿A qué destino debería reservar un vuelo en estos momentos?

chunks.claim: Hopper ships a family of flexibility products, not a single one.
Hopper's web surface permits search but gates its differentiating products behind the app.
AirCover is included in every accommodation booking at no cost. It is the opposite commercial model to Hopper's Premium Disruption Assistance, for the same category of promise.
chunks.evidence: Todas las reservas de alojamientos incluyen AirCover para huéspedes

chunks.claim: Airbnb states what AirCover is NOT, in plain language, with concrete examples — inside the same document that sells the reassurance.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma proposes to cover the WHOLE journey. AirCover demonstrates that a bounded promise, stated honestly, is more trustworthy than an unbounded one. The transferable technique is not the coverage — it is publishing the edge of the coverage in the same breath as the coverage.
chunks.evidence: AirCover para huéspedes no es una póliza de seguro. No cubre problemas relacionados con el viaje (por ejemplo, si tu viaje se retrasa debido a una tormenta o si tu equipaje resulta dañado por tu compañía aérea)

chunks.claim: Placed together, Airbnb and Hopper cover opposite halves of the journey and neither covers the seam.
chunks.confidence: Verified as a description of the two products' stated scopes. The consequence is Inferred — no traveller was observed in this state.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is a narrower and more defensible opportunity than 'own the whole chain'. The seam between a covered flight and a covered stay is uncovered by both specialists, and it exists only because the two bookings are separate objects. Luma proposes to model the trip as ONE object — which is the only structure in which that seam can be closed.

chunks.claim: Airbnb offers no sort control at all. It is the only competitor observed with none.
chunks.why_it_matters: Airbnb gives the traveller filters but not ordering. You accept its ranking or you refine the set. For a first-time traveller that is arguably kinder — fewer decisions — and arguably worse: no recourse if the ranking does not suit you, and no visibility into why it ranked that way. Booking.com offers 11 ways to reorder and explains none of them; Airbnb offers zero and likewise explains nothing.
chunks.scope_limit: The 'Filtros' panel was NOT opened. If a sort lives inside it, this finding narrows to 'no sort on the results surface'. Recorded as a limit on the claim, not a hedge on the sweep.

chunks.claim: Airbnb displays the total price for the stay and never a nightly rate. Every other accommodation competitor observed leads with a nightly figure.
chunks.why_it_matters: Nightly pricing is the industry's standard way of making a stay look cheaper than it is — the traveller multiplies, and the fees arrive later. Airbnb removes that arithmetic entirely at the point of comparison. For a first-time traveller who does not yet know that a €112 night is really €450, this is the single most useful pricing decision observed in the round, and it costs nothing to adopt.
chunks.evidence: Prices render as '203 € en total', '199 € en total', '270 € en total', '244 € en total'. Full page swept for 'por noche', '/ noche', 'noche' — ZERO matches.

chunks.claim: Airbnb offers travel insurance at checkout with a neutral, priced question. Expedia phrases the same decision as a confession of recklessness.
chunks.why_it_matters: Both products attach insurance at the same point in the same journey for comparable amounts. One manufactures guilt; one asks. This is the clearest paired evidence in the round that the dark pattern is a CHOICE, not a requirement of the economics — because a larger competitor declines to use it at the identical moment.
chunks.evidence: ¿Quieres añadir un seguro de viaje? Sí, quiero añadirlo por 9,32 €

chunks.claim: Airbnb offers three payment timings, one of which defers the entire cost at no additional charge.
chunks.why_it_matters: A first-time traveller on a limited budget faces a commitment they cannot easily reverse. 'Pay 0 € now, charged 28 Oct, no additional costs' reduces the cost of committing without selling them debt. That distinction — deferral versus credit — is worth making explicitly.

chunks.claim: Airbnb states whether the price is normal, at the moment of payment.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-27 recorded that Google is the only product telling a traveller what a normal price looks like — but Google does it BEFORE the search. Airbnb does it at CHECKOUT, the moment of maximum doubt. Same orientation device, opposite end of the journey. Neither Booking.com nor Expedia offers it at either point.
chunks.evidence: El precio está por debajo de la media para 60 días

chunks.claim: Airbnb gives the traveller no way to reorder results and the most detailed explanation of its ordering found anywhere in the round.
chunks.why_it_matters: Control and explanation are being treated as alternatives across this market, and nobody offers both. The unoccupied position is few axes, well explained — which is also the kinder position for a traveller who does not know what to sort by.

chunks.claim: Airbnb states that its algorithm deliberately favours variety — showing different hosts, characteristics and price points rather than the single best-scoring set.
chunks.why_it_matters: No other competitor states a diversity objective in its ranking. Every other observed ranking optimises a single dimension or an opaque composite. For a traveller who does not yet know what they want — Luma's stated user — a deliberately varied first page is arguably more useful than a strictly optimal one, because it teaches the shape of the market rather than answering a question they cannot yet ask.
chunks.evidence: El algoritmo también favorece la variedad y muestra a los viajeros anuncios de distintos anfitriones y con diferentes características y precios

chunks.claim: The five stated factors contain no commission, advertising or paid-placement term.
chunks.confidence: Verified as an observation about the DOCUMENT.
chunks.scope_limit: This establishes what Airbnb SAYS about its ranking. It does not establish that no commercial factor exists — an omission from a help article is not evidence of absence in an algorithm. Recorded strictly as a difference in DISCLOSURE, not in behaviour.

chunks.claim: Airbnb holds stays, experiences and services under one account and still does not model the trip as a single object. Moving from an accommodation search to experiences drops the trip entirely.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the strongest available evidence that business goal 2 is UNSOLVED rather than merely unclaimed. It also reframes the difficulty: the barrier is not inventory or accounts — Airbnb has both — it is that nobody has modelled the trip as the object the traveller actually has. That is a data-model decision made before any screen is designed.

chunks.claim: Airbnb shows accommodation as a total for the stay and experiences as a price per traveller. The same product uses two conventions in two verticals.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-70 credited Airbnb with removing the arithmetic a traveller must do. That credit holds for stays and does not extend to experiences: a party of two now multiplies again, and 'desde' (from) reintroduces a floor price that is not the price. The convention that makes stays legible is abandoned in the vertical the traveller reaches second.

chunks.claim: Tripadvisor's primary entry point is a question rather than a search field label.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-61 established that three competitors ASSERT the traveller's location and none asks. This is the same distinction at the other end: a product that opens with a question rather than a command. For a low-confidence user the difference between 'Enter destination' and 'Where are you going?' is small in words and large in posture.
chunks.evidence: ¿Adónde vas?

chunks.claim: 'Descubrir' (Discover) is a top-level navigation item, alongside 'Opinión' (Review).
chunks.why_it_matters: This confirms the roster rationale for Tripadvisor — it was included as the product assumed to lead with discovery rather than a search box, covering the scenario's stage 1 'Dream & discover'. It does. Discovery is a place you can go, not a state you pass through on the way to a search.
chunks.evidence: Primary nav: Descubrir · Opinión · Más. Vertical tabs: Cosas que hacer · Hoteles · Restaurantes.

chunks.claim: Tripadvisor's primary verticals are things to do, hotels and restaurants. No flights vertical was present on the homepage.
chunks.scope_limit: Homepage only. A flights surface may exist elsewhere on the site.

chunks.claim: Two extraction sweeps on this page returned TRAVELLER REVIEW TEXT. A 'filterGroups' selector aimed at headings pulled review titles, and a 'cancellationSignals' regex pulled a complaint about a failed booking modification.
Tripadvisor surfaces activity duration — but only inside seller-written titles, never as a structured, comparable field.
chunks.why_it_matters: Effort is structured where it is easy to measure and unstructured where it is not — the same pattern as the F-25 correction, now visible one layer down. Flights compute duration; activity operators type it into a title. Luma's on-site activity layer would be the first to make it a field.
evidence: De Sintra a Cascais: 2 palacios, 7 lugares de interés, excursión de 10 horas en grupo reducido
Verdadero Tour Privado Tuk Tuk de 4 Horas
Tour Privado Tuk Tuk de Lisboa y Recogida en el hotel : 2, 3, o 4 Horas
Excursión de 2 horas al atardecer en Lisboa

chunks.claim: Tripadvisor states the basis of its rankings on the results surface.
chunks.evidence: Estas clasificaciones se basan en los datos de Tripadvisor: tenemos en cuenta las opiniones de los viajeros, las puntua[ciones]...

chunks.claim: Rentalcars.com states on its own homepage that it is part of Booking Holdings — the same parent as Booking.com, competitor 1.
chunks.confidence: Verified — first-party statement on the product's own homepage.
chunks.evidence: Rentalcars.com es parte de Booking Holdings Inc., líder mundial en viajes online y servicios relacionados.

chunks.claim: Rentalcars makes an explicit no-hidden-charges claim on the homepage.
chunks.confidence: Verified that the CLAIM is made. NOT verified that it holds — no booking flow was walked, and car hire is the vertical where counter-desk charges, fuel policy, insurance excess and deposits classically appear after the headline price.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the third distinct position on price honesty observed. Google Flights commits to all-in pricing with a named exception (F-30). Kayak explicitly excludes baggage (F-46). Rentalcars asserts no hidden charges without naming an exception at all — the strongest claim and the least qualified.
chunks.evidence: Sin cargos ocultos

chunks.claim: The cancellation promise carries a qualifier that most travellers will not weigh.
chunks.why_it_matters: Compare Airbnb, which states a DATE — 'Cancelación gratuita antes del 5 de noviembre' — and Iberia, which distinguishes voluntary from operational and names the difference (F-56). 'La mayoría' is a promise a traveller cannot check against their own booking at the moment they read it. For Luma's stated user, an unresolvable qualifier is worse than a smaller specific promise.
chunks.evidence: Cancelación gratuita en la mayoría de las reservas

chunks.claim: Trainline offers to notify the traveller when they QUALIFY FOR DELAY COMPENSATION — not merely when a delay occurs.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest, most transferable disruption feature observed in the entire round. It requires no inventory, no balance sheet and no insurance licence — only knowing the traveller's itinerary and the compensation rules. Luma's scenario already assumes it holds the itinerary. This is the strongest single candidate for 'reducing travel stress' that is both unoccupied in air and already proven in rail.
evidence: Get notified instantly in case of delay or cancellation.
Get notified when you qualify for delay compensation.

chunks.claim: Trainline's search form carries a PRE-CHECKED Booking.com Genius cross-sell which, on search, opened a Booking.com hotel search in the original tab — with dates that are not the travel dates.
Trainline surfaces duration and change-count per result and offers a 'Direct only' filter.
evidence: 3h 23m, 0 changes

chunks.claim: Trainline states its ranking basis and leads with two effort criteria before price.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the working proof that an effort-first ranking is buildable and explicable in one sentence. The objection to 'easiest first' has been that effort cannot be computed. In rail it is computed, ranked FIRST, and explained in twenty-six words.
chunks.evidence: We show tickets for the fastest available journeys with the smallest number of changes, highlighting the cheapest within these results. Some results may be sponsored.

chunks.claim: A search for Madrid to Barcelona could not be completed. A cookie consent modal — 'Administrar preferencias de cookies' — intercepted the input and blocked the search form.
Omio's consent modal states it shares personal data with 164 partners.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario names GDPR-adjacent obligations only implicitly, via 'Accessibility compliant' and multi-language constraints. This is a concrete measure of what a travel intermediary's data surface actually looks like — and the number is stated by the vendor, not estimated. A first-time traveller consenting here is consenting across 164 organisations. Luma's own partner count is a design decision with the same visibility consequence.
chunks.evidence: Nosotros y nuestros 164 socios tratamos tus datos personales mediante cookies y tecnologías similares

chunks.claim: Omio accepts city, station, airport OR port in a single origin field and compares across four transport modes in one result set.
chunks.why_it_matters: This is the most direct answer observed to the scenario's own opening problem — 'Comparing flights, transport, accommodation and activities happens in different places and never lines up.' Omio makes four transport modes line up in one query. Trainline compares train and bus (270 companies); Omio adds air and ferry across 2,000. The single field accepting four location TYPES is the concrete mechanism — the traveller does not have to know which mode they want before they can search.

chunks.claim: Omio ships an AI planner as a primary tab beside the standard search — 'Planificador IA'.
chunks.why_it_matters: The prior round listed 'assistant commoditisation' as a standing risk. It is no longer a risk — it is the baseline. Luma cannot position on having an AI planner.

chunks.claim: Rome2Rio presents duration and price together, per transport mode, in one view — including modes no other roster competitor surfaces.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-42 credited Kayak with showing the trade-off ON the sort control — price and duration together, so €12 buying back 5h49m is visible before choosing. Rome2Rio does the same thing ACROSS MODES: 3h2m at one price against 8h5m at another, with the cheapest marked. A traveller can see that eight hours of coach saves a specific amount of money, without running three searches on three sites.

chunks.claim: Rome2Rio surfaces no booking or purchase language on the comparison view — consistent with the roster's assumption that it routes and compares without fulfilling.
chunks.confidence: Verified for the rendered surface; the load caveat applies.

chunks.claim: Citymapper presents transit options with frequency, calories and cross-mode alternatives alongside price and duration — three attributes absent from every other competitor in the roster.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma's Core Features list includes 'Arrival transport to the accommodation' at stage 5 and 'Transport on site — routes, tickets, passes' at stage 6. This capture is the working reference for both, and it demonstrates that the useful attributes at that moment are NOT the ones the booking products optimise for.

chunks.claim: Across the roster, effort is now observed measured in three different units, and which unit is used depends entirely on what the vertical can compute.
TripIt models the trip as one object — and does so by ingesting other products' confirmations, without selling anything.
chunks.why_it_matters: Luma proposes to do both: sell the components AND hold the single trip view. No observed competitor does both. TripIt proves the view is buildable without inventory; Booking.com and Expedia prove inventory does not produce the view. Whether one product can hold both is the central unanswered question of this round.

chunks.claim: TripIt's organisation is free; the features that address traveller anxiety are behind TripIt Pro.
chunks.why_it_matters: The paywalled list maps almost exactly onto Luma's own Core Features: 'Live flight tracking', 'Gate notifications', 'Airport shopping and food recommendations', 'Entry requirements'. Four of Luma's named features are TripIt's paid tier.

chunks.claim: TripIt sells pre-trip entry-requirement guidance as a named Pro feature.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario's stage 4 'Prepare' names 'Travel documents' and 'Entry requirements' as Luma capabilities, and its user list includes 'International travellers — visas, entry requirements, languages, currencies, connectivity'. This is the first observed competitor addressing that user type directly. F-59 recorded Iberia as the first to address families; this is the second of the scenario's five user types to be addressed by anything in the roster.
chunks.evidence: Even the most frequent flyer faces uncertainty when navigating international travel requirements. TripIt is taking the guesswork out of pre-trip requirements

chunks.claim: The meta-search handoff deposits the traveller, pre-selected, into the airline's most restrictive fare family.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-49 established that protection varies across a Kayak result set and is never displayed. This shows the mechanism completing: the cheapest path is not merely less protected in the abstract, it ARRIVES pre-committed to the least flexible fare, described to the traveller as their own decision. A first-time traveller who clicked 'cheapest' has now, without a further choice, selected the fare with the least change and cancellation freedom.
chunks.decision_for_luma: Decision required: if Luma hands off, does it hand off to a CHOICE or to a pre-selected commitment? Kayak's convenience here is also the removal of a decision the traveller did not know they were making.

chunks.claim: Iberia states an all-in total with a named exception. Kayak, which sent the traveller here, states that its prices exclude baggage fees.
chunks.why_it_matters: The supplier is more honest about price construction than the comparison layer above it — and names the specific exception rather than gesturing at one. This inverts the assumption that intermediaries protect travellers from supplier opacity. On price, the opposite held here.

chunks.claim: Iberia's airport services are bundled with Business class, not sold as add-ons. The page title scopes them to a fare class in its own words.
chunks.scope_limit: One airline, one page, Spanish market. American Airlines and Qatar are untouched and may sell these separately — that is exactly what tier 4 was widened to test.

chunks.claim: Business goal 5 assumes airport services are a purchasable product. On the first supplier examined they are a fare-class entitlement, which changes who Luma would be selling to.
chunks.confidence: Verified as an observation about Iberia; the market inference is Inferred, from this single capture.
decision_for_luma: Decision required: is Luma selling airport services to economy travellers — competing with lounge aggregators nobody has analysed — or surfacing entitlements travellers already hold and do not know about? The second is a reassurance feature and needs no inventory. The first is a business Luma has not scoped.

Decision required: Luma's stated user is a first-time traveller on a limited budget. They are not in Business class. Goal 5 and the target user may be pulling in opposite directions, and that should be settled before design.

chunks.claim: Iberia ships a chat assistant, 'Ibot', present on this page.

chunks.claim: Iberia explicitly distinguishes voluntary changes from operational disruption, states that the traveller's rights are different, and then provides no route to them.
chunks.evidence: La información de esta página está enfocada a cambios y reembolsos voluntarios. Si tu viaje se ha visto afectado por causas operativas, tus derechos y las opciones disponibles son diferentes

chunks.claim: Traced end to end, the traveller's protection degrades at every hop and is never displayed at any of them.
chunks.confidence: Verified — each link in the chain is an individually verified capture in this round.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario's business objective is 'reducing travel stress and helping users confidently navigate every stage'. This chain IS the stress, and no participant in it is lying or failing individually — each is behaving reasonably within its own scope. The gap is that nobody holds the whole chain. That is the clearest statement of Luma's opportunity produced by this round, and it is evidenced at five points across five products.

chunks.claim: Iberia Club is the only loyalty programme of the three examined whose currency can be earned without travelling at all.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-18 established that both OTA programmes gate their value behind accumulated bookings, which a first-time traveller by definition does not have. This is the first observed programme that solves that: a traveller can arrive at their FIRST booking already holding balance. It is the only mechanism seen in the round that gives a zero-history user something real on day one.
chunks.evidence: Acumular puntos Iberia Club es muy fácil: te regalamos Avios cada vez que realices una compra en más de 90 marcas asociadas al programa

chunks.claim: Iberia Club extends programme benefits to children as a stated feature.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario names five primary user types, one of which is 'Families travelling with children — coordinating several people, luggage and routines'. This is the FIRST observed competitor feature addressed at that user type anywhere in the round. Neither Genius nor One Key made any reference to children or family accounts.
chunks.evidence: Las ventajas de Iberia Club, también para niños

chunks.claim: Three loyalty programmes, three full-page text searches, zero mentions of a first-time traveller.
chunks.evidence: Searched this page for 'primer viaje', 'nuevo socio', 'principiante', 'primera vez' — no match. Same null previously recorded for Genius (F-02) and One Key (F-18).

chunks.claim: American Airlines publishes a Customer Service Plan containing explicitly named disruption sections.
chunks.why_it_matters: This matters because it removes an excuse. 'Disruption is a legal matter, not a product surface' does not survive the pair. One carrier chose to document its commitments in plain sections; the other chose to name the regime and stop. Both are choices, and Luma has the same choice.

chunks.claim: I ran the symmetric findability sweep on AA using ENGLISH terms — delay, cancel, disrupt, compensat, rights, irregular, service plan, refund — against a page served in SPANISH. It returned zero matches for every category including loyalty and lounges, which should have been the tell.
aa.com redirects to americanairlines.es for a Spanish-locale session, serving a materially thinner site — 43 links against a US site that hosts a full Customer Service Plan.
chunks.why_it_matters: The scenario requires 'Multi-language support' as a constraint. This is what it looks like when a carrier implements localisation as a SEPARATE, thinner site rather than a translation: capability silently disappears by market. A traveller's access to disruption help depends on which country they load the page from.

chunks.claim: AA's Spanish homepage surfaces travel disruption prominently — as a heading, not a buried link.
evidence: Actualizaciones de viaje (heading)
Alertas de viaje (link, appearing twice)
Estado del vuelo (link)

chunks.claim: Qatar Airways sells the loyalty currency, the STATUS points, and a paid subscription to the loyalty programme itself.
chunks.confidence: Verified that these products exist as named destinations. Their mechanics and prices were NOT captured.
chunks.why_it_matters: F-58 identified the transferable idea as separating a SPENDABLE currency open to everyone from a STATUS ladder earned by use. Qatar collapses that separation entirely — status is a product. That is the logical endpoint of tenure-based loyalty and it is worth Luma seeing, because it shows the model's destination: if status can be bought, it no longer signals anything about the traveller, and the first-time traveller can simply pay to skip the ladder. Whether that is a feature or the death of the mechanism is a genuine strategic question.

chunks.claim: Qatar Airways treats the airport as a destination with its own product line, unlike Iberia where airport services are a Business-class entitlement.
chunks.confidence: Verified that these destinations exist. Whether any is PURCHASABLE by an economy passenger was NOT determined — no pricing page was opened.

chunks.claim: No disruption, delay, cancellation, compensation or passenger-rights destination appears in Qatar Airways' 289 homepage links.
chunks.why_it_matters: Across three airlines, the moment a traveller most needs help is the moment hardest to navigate to. That is the consistent observation of the entire round — F-56, F-57, F-90, F-104 and now F-107 all point at the same gap from different angles.

chunks.claim: Lounge access sits at Silver — the first tier above entry — and Qpoints, the currency that reaches Silver, are sold by Qatar Airways.
chunks.confidence: Verified that both facts hold. The INFERENCE that one can buy enough Qpoints to reach Silver is Inferred — purchase limits and whether bought Qpoints count toward tier qualification were NOT captured, and many programmes explicitly exclude purchased points from tier progression.

chunks.claim: Privilege Club runs three distinct currencies.
chunks.why_it_matters: Complexity scales with the operator's ability to monetise it. Luma at ideation has no basis for three currencies and, per F-58, its user starts at zero on all of them. The transferable observation is NOT the currency design — it is that every one of these programmes measures the same thing: money spent with the operator. None measures whether the traveller had a good trip.

chunks.claim: Four loyalty programmes, four full-text searches, zero mentions of a first-time traveller.
chunks.evidence: This page searched for 'first-time', 'new member', 'beginner', 'just starting' — no match. Same null recorded for Genius (F-02), One Key (F-18) and Iberia Club (F-60).

chunks.claim: F-108 inferred that lounge access is indirectly purchasable, because lounge access sits at Silver and Qpoints are sold — but flagged that many programmes exclude PURCHASED points from tier qualification, and that the inference was unverified.
chunks.confidence: Verified for the mechanism and the unit price. UNKNOWN for the caps.

chunks.claim: Qatar Airways publishes a unit price for loyalty status: USD 25 per Qpoint.
chunks.why_it_matters: It converts a strategic question into an arithmetic one. If status is worth USD 25 a point to the operator, the operator is telling you what the benefit bundle is worth to it — and by implication what it costs to give away. For Luma, which proposes to grant reassurance to travellers who have earned nothing, this is the closest thing to a market price on the thing being given away.
